Sports.title: Wales v New Zealand: Chance to make a statement against All Blacks
Sports.text:
Andy Haden's dive, Joe Rokocoko's try double in a tight thriller, Alun Wyn Jones running out of steam after an interception, Andrew Hore getting away with a first-minute punch. What Wales would give for another sob story against New Zealand.

Steve Tandy's side have the latest shot at making history when they welcome the All Blacks to Principality Stadium in the Nations Championship (14:10 GMT).

The odds for a home win are long: 20-1.

That is the same price as Japan at England, while bookies prefer Fiji's chances in Ireland.

The likelihood is a 35th straight loss to New Zealand will be chalked up, with the streak of Welsh misery going into a 74th year since the victory in December 1953.

Tickets are still available for the fixture, which would have been unthinkable in past years when supporters feared missing history being made.

Is it defeatist to consider what would be a successful loss?

After spluttering to a 28-21 victory against Japan, and with morale low in the Welsh game courtesy of constant off-field turmoil, Wales must show something.

A year ago the score in the 48th minute was just 24-21 to New Zealand. Can Tandy's men make it to the hour with the unlikely still possible?

Head coach Tandy has enjoyed victories against Japan twice, Fiji and Italy since taking the reins in 2025.

Wales' most recent victory of real significance was the 40-6 dismantling of Australia in the group stages of the 2023 World Cup under Warren Gatland.

The Wallabies are in town next Saturday (20:10 GMT) and that appears to present a better chance for a statement win, especially after their shocker against England last weekend.

Number eight Aaron Wainwright, who will be missed against New Zealand due to injury, stressed before the campaign that it is time to start making others sit up and take notice.

"It's about now we need to start putting in those performances that are going to make teams worried about us," he said before Wales failed to do that against Japan.

Wales were ranked eighth in the world when edged out 26-25 by New Zealand in 2004, a defeat that came a fortnight after a 38-36 loss to South Africa.

With 11 months to the start of the 2027 Rugby World Cup, time is running out to earn the respect of the teams that will travel to Australia with hopes of lifting the trophy.

"We want to push up the the rankings table, we want to get back into the top eight," said Wales captain Dewi Lake.

"You're looking at two teams [in New Zealand and Australia] that are sitting in there. It's an opportunity to see how we measure up."

The display against Japan did little to suggest that the gap to the elite is closing.

The mood in the Wales camp is upbeat and there is belief that progress is being made under Tandy and his new-look coaching team, albeit baby steps need to turn into strides.

"We were lucky last week that we were good enough to still win the game off the back of not performing as well as we wanted," admitted Lake.

"We've done a lot of work over the last year and a half on performance and we want to see that come to fruition.

"We know there are more levels in us and need to go there this weekend."

Tandy has tinkered with his team, with Wainwright's injury presenting a big opportunity for Taine Basham to take his Cardiff club form on to the international stage.

The 27-year-old from Talywain was Wales' star man against New Zealand in 2021 and this will be his first Test start since 2022.

The dynamic back-row forward must grasp his opportunity in the most fiercely competitive department of the squad.

Wales stick with the heavyweight centre partnership of Max Llewellyn and Eddie James, with the pressure on the set-piece to provide more of a platform.

The line-out struggled against Japan - who have top operators in Harry Hockings, Warner Dearns and Ben Gunter - but hooker Lake is confident it was just a bad day.

"Go back on our performances over the last 12 to 18 months and we've been one of the top teams in the world in that area," said the Gloucester captain.

"A lot of our tries have come from driving maul or line-out set plays. We have got backs who are dangerous on launch plays.

"When we do secure our set-piece we are a dangerous team. It was a setback last week but we'll put it right."

Montpellier lock Adam Beard, who is 6ft 8ins, returns to the side as line-out caller and Dragons co-captain Ben Carter drops to the bench.

Wales scored four tries in defeat by New Zealand last year when Tom Rogers made history with a hat-trick, with his fellow wing Louis Rees-Zammit getting the other with an acrobatic finish.

Rees-Zammit and full-back Blair Murray will aim to build on bright showings against Japan and have been joined by in-form Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb in the bid to give New Zealand a bloody nose.

"When you get the ball and get chances, be brave with it, be fearless because we have a strong back line and players who can finish," said Rees-Zammit.

Wales have only finished within a score of the All Blacks twice in 23 games since rugby union went professional in 1995.

In 2004 the defeat was by a point, with poor time management proving costly at the end, while in 2009 a chance to end the losing streak with a draw was lost when lock Jones was reeled in after an interception and then a last-gasp line-out went awry.

Better Wales teams than this one - Grand Slam winners and sides full of Lions - have failed to put the All Blacks under pressure.

New Zealand are hunting their fourth successive half-century in Cardiff after a 54-16 win in 2021, 55-23 in 2022 and 52-26 last year.

The second of those triumphs matched the All Blacks' highest points tally against Wales, a number they first hit in Hamilton in 2003.

It is a very one-sided rivalry but the magic of facing New Zealand, and facing the Haka, remains.

"I remember the 2013 year that they went unbeaten. They were a special team and will probably go down as the greatest ever," said lock Dafydd Jenkins about the double World Cup winning side.

"Everyone loved watching them. Brodie Retallick, Sam Whitelock, Kieran Read, Jerome Kaino and Richie McCaw – that back five will go down in history.

"When I was growing up, they were the South Africa of today and everyone hears stories about the famous black jersey.

"I've played with a few Kiwis at Exeter and they say how important it is to their culture. There's an aura around the All Blacks jersey."

The mood surrounding New Zealand is vastly different to 2025, when they travelled to Wales fresh from defeat by England.

The pressure and scrutiny on then boss Scott Robertson was intense as he twitchily carried out his pre-match media duties in their Cardiff bay hotel.

New Zealand eased to victory at Principality Stadium but it proved to be Robertson's last game in charge.

Dave Rennie was brought in as head coach and the former Glasgow boss appears to have made an immediate impact in game plan, clarity and culture.

New Zealand beat South Africa in Johannesburg and took plenty of positives despite being hit by a Springbok response in three defeats that followed.

After two wins against Australia and last week's second-half dominance against Scotland, the All Blacks will expect to ease past Wales before a mouthwatering game against England that is seen as the litmus test of their progress.

Beauden Barrett, who will captain New Zealand in a Test for the first time, warned against complacency.

"Wales are a team that want to play," said the full-back. "They've got plenty of excitement and some really big threats, especially out wide.

"They've certainly got a lot of grit, a lot of skill and X-factor, so we've got to be ready for anything."

New Zealand aim to keep the heat on South Africa for first place in the southern hemisphere table, although the world champions have a healthy points difference advantage.

Wales players will back themselves to reward those who put their money on the 20-1 long shot, but most outside the camp would settle for making the visitors work for victory.

Wales have two fixtures remaining to decide their placing for finals day at Allianz Stadium.

It is possible that they could learn their Twickenham opponents this weekend with a round to play.

If Italy fail to beat Argentina with a bonus point on Saturday (11:40 GMT) then Wales will be guaranteed to finish at least fifth in the northern hemisphere table.

A Scotland bonus-point win against Australia on Sunday (15:10 GMT) would put fourth out of reach, and the Scots finish against Japan even if they slip up.

Wales are likely to finish fifth and play on Saturday, 28 November (13:10 GMT) in a double-header with the teams that finish second.

Another meeting with Japan looms unless Fiji win in Italy next weekend.

Gaming_Tech.title: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
Gaming_Tech.text:
A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.

The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.

The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running".

"For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.

The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.

Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.

The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect, knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.

Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack.

Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".

"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
Gaming_Tech.text:
A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world.

Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced.

Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption.

Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.

Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.

From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.

But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues.

As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.

The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".

In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.

"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.

Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".

In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.

Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".

The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.

When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.

Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.

Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.

"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.

"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.

"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.

"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."

The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".

He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.

Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.

"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.

Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.

In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.

The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.

Gaming_Tech.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
Gaming_Tech.text:
How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The answer is very.

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.

But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?

That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.

A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.

Other senior officials wanted a tougher response.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.

Now the political pressure is building.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.

And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.

Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.

The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.

It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".

That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?

The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.

This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

Gaming_Tech.title: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for not banning Nvidia chip sales to China-linked firm
Gaming_Tech.text:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.

There is growing pressure on Lutnick across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.

However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.

"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.

"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?

"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."

Gaming_Tech.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?

Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.

From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.

But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".

So how much AI enhancement is too much?

Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.

But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.

"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."

For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.

It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.

But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.

"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."

All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.

Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.

It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.

According to a recent survey, external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.

Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.

He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.

But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.

"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."

He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.

Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.

In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.

In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.

Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.

"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.

Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.

But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.

He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.

"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

Gaming_Tech.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
Gaming_Tech.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.

"The American people deserve answers," he added.

Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.

Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.

It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.

Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.

Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.

Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.

The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.

Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.

Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.

Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.

Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.

Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

Gaming_Tech.title: Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.

The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.

We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.

Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.

Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.

She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.

But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.

Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.

Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.

Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.

Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.

"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.

Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.

Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.

Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.

Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.

US President Donald Trump suggested Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, as a good replacement.

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" he wrote on Truth Social.

Liu said Cook could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.

Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".

Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."

Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.

"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
Gaming_Tech.text:
At least 74 countries were affected by the Microsoft outage which was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, all experienced "connectivity problems", the company said.

As of early Friday afternoon (GMT), Microsoft was reporting improvements, with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption was widespread. Here is what happened around the world.

In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico, external their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems.

OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.

Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.

The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.

"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."

In Canada, a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.

The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.

Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.

Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers might not be able to receive emails about their trips because of the outage.

Disruptions were also reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.

In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times, external.

The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.

Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".

Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.

In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".

In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.

Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.

Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.

European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.

Speaking to the same news agency, the head of Germany's BSI cybersecurity agency, Claudia Plattner, said the country's authorities had not been affected because they did not rely on Microsoft 365 services.

However, Reuters reported that Germany's national rail operator, Deutsche Bahn, was having difficulties sending out timetables for diverted trains due to the outage.

Plattner added the disruption was "affecting the whole world". "It is a global disruption that spans a vast number of data centres – stretching from Asia right across to the US, via Europe," she said.

In Antalya, Turkey, advisers and officials attending the UN Climate Change Conference, Cop31, were left frustrated by the outage.

James Young, a climate change adviser at the Inuit Circumpolar Council, the organisation which represents around 180,000 Inuit people living in the Arctic, told Reuters the council relied on emails and Microsoft Teams to communicate across several countries.

"It's just been really frustrating and challenging to maintain contact with our colleagues and to be able to effectively participate here," he said. "I think our dependence on technology leaves us vulnerable to situations like this."

In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies were among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.

"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa were unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.

However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

One winemaker in South Africa said almost his entire business had been brought to a "standstill" by the Microsoft outage.

"It's incredibly frustrating," Peter Pentz added. "We export a lot, so communication with exporters in Europe has come to a standstill."

Order processing, dispatch, communications and even "critical production work" were halted, he said, as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Gaming_Tech.title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
Gaming_Tech.text:
Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.

Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.

NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.

Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.

The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.

The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.

Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.

The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.

NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.

Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".

The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.

There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.

The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.

Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.

In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".

Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.

That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.

Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments.

Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties.

Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normal

MPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place

The Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outage

MSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent casework

Some businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp.

Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over.

But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools.

Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices.

Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed.

"We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said.

Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match.

Gaming_Tech.title: Global Microsoft outage affecting tens of thousands of users
Gaming_Tech.text:
Microsoft is struggling to fix a major global outageof its service that is reportedly affecting tens of thousands of users.

Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot have been affected by "connectivity problems".

The company said in a series of updates on X that it was seeing "positive results" with its efforts to restore services and that it was rushing to fix the problem.

Reports of issues with Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector. The BBC understands there is no indication the outage was caused by a cyber-attack.

The disruption affects programs that are part of Microsoft 365 - a popular online service among businesses that allows them to use workplace tools like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive.

For international organisations, this platform is essential for connecting and collaborating with colleagues around the world.

Among the issues, users may be unable to view certain files or details on their calendar apps, Microsoft said.

Its AI platform, Copilot, may also be unable to work properly.

Messaging and online meetings were largely functional, the firm added.

Microsoft said on X that the outage was caused by a number of servers "being unexpectedly unavailable", straining its remaining systems.

"We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible," said a Microsoft spokesperson.

The company later warned that some services that had been restored "can become unresponsive again", adding that customers "in any region" could be affected.

Users around the world including the US, Japan and Singapore have reported facing disruptions.

Gaming_Tech.title: Firm offers to fake artworks for wealthy migrants seeking UK 'talent' visas - BBC investigation
Gaming_Tech.text:
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.

The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.

Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.

We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.

No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.

In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.

A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.

"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.

The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.

A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".

They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:

At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying

The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application

For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.

The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.

A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".

Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".

The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.

About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.

The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.

Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".

Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.

"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.

Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.

Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.

During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.

The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.

It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.

Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.

This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.

Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.

The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.

The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.

During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.

The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.

"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."

He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".

When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.

"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".

"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."

The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".

Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.

The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.

The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".

It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.

Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.

"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."

Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.

Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.

The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.

Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.

If you would like to contact our team about this story you can email on: politicsinvestigations@bbc.co.uk, external

Additional reporting by Ruhua Xianyu

Entertainment.title: Eurovision Song Contest is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up in Thailand
Entertainment.text:
On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.

And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.

It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.

Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.

"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.

"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.

"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.

This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.

Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.

Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.

There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.

A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.

Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.

The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.

Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.

The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".

In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.

Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.

For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.

"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."

Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988.

Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets.

Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest.

Entertainment.text:
Timothée Chalamet and his Dune co-stars will be seen pranking Rylan Clark during this year's Children in Need on Friday.

The Oscar-nominated actor will be seen making the presenter sweat with suggestions from children behind-the-scenes in an Impractical Jokers-style set-up, during an interview with Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy about the third installment of the film franchise.

This year's Children in Need show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Last year's appeal raised more than £45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.

The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They will welcome Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.

Wyn Evans completed his 400-mile four-nation cycle ride through England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and his native Wales - finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

He raised more than £3.8m along the way.

Entertainment.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
Entertainment.text:
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.

The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.

La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."

The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."

Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.

She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.

The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.

He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.

Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.

Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".

"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.

She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.

Entertainment.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says US move humbled her before big break with Steven Spielberg
Entertainment.text:
Catherine Zeta-Jones has said she had an ego check after moving to America in the 1990s.

The Swansea-born star had become a household name in the UK, but Hollywood quickly provided a reality check for the rising star and she was even asked by casting agents if she had any acting experience.

It was during her stint on CBS mini-series Titanic that she was seen by Steven Spielberg who suggested she go for a role in The Mask of Zorro which he was producing.

"Five days later I got the job, and three days after that, I was down there starting my sword-fighting lessons," she said.

Zeta-Jones had become a star in the UK thanks to her breakout role in The Darling Buds of May that originally aired from 1991 to 1993.

But when she touched down in California, she was no longer recognised by the public and had a six-month visa to "give America a shot".

But Zeta-Jones told Business Insider it was "good" for her to have her ego knocked down a bit.

It was only when the Spielberg saw the Titanic series that she was given a major opportunity.

"I was shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas," she said.

Entertainment.title: Download 2027 line-up: Blink-182 to headline on festival debut
Entertainment.text:
Blink-182, Evanescence & Bring Me The Horizon have been announced as headliners of next year's Download Festival.

The trio are among more than 100 rock and metal acts set to play the event at Donington Park, Leicestershire from 9 to 13 June.

Other acts on the bill include The Prodigy, 5 Seconds of Summer and a special performance by heavy metal legends Mötley Crüe.

US pop-punk band Blink-182 will be making their Download debut, while Evanescence will become the festival's second female-fronted headliner.

The American rock band were founded by singer Amy Lee in the mid-1990s and had a UK number one with their best-known single Bring Me to Life in 2003.

It's the second year in a row a female-led band has headlined the festival, after Linkin Park topped the bill in 2025.

The nu-metal group have reformed with Emily Armstrong as their lead singer, after the death of former frontman Chester Bennington, who took his own life in 2017.

The choice of Emily upset some fans, who pointed to her alleged ties to the Church of Scientology and past support for convicted rapist Danny Masterson - someone she distanced herself from.

Next year's Download will be a first for Blink-182, who emerged from the California skate punk scene in the 1990s.

They've had two UK top 10 singles and had their first number one album in 2016, 21 years after their first record.

Their drummer Travis Barker is married to Kourtney Kardashian and survived a plane crash in the US that killed four people in 2008.

British rockers Bring Me The Horizon are more familiar to Download regulars, headlining for the second time in five years.

The four-piece band, formed in Sheffield, announced earlier this year they're celebrating 20 years of the debut album Count Your Blessings by re-recording it.

That 2006 record was in the deathcore genre, known for its heavy and aggressive sound, but the band have since moved towards metalcore, pop and electronic rock.

Some fans questioned if the original lyrics, which frontman Oli Sykes admitted could be interpreted as misogynistic, were still appropriate.

But the 39-year-old lead vocalist told the BBC Radio 1 Rock Show that going back to their roots was "a lot of fun" as they "got to remake the album how we wanted it to sound back then".

Entertainment.title: Duran Duran's Roger Taylor quits Birmingham band over tinnitus
Entertainment.text:
Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor said he will leave the band due to his worsening tinnitus.

Taylor has been the chart-topping group's drummer since they formed in Birmingham in 1978, which he described as "the joy of my life", but said he had "reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors".

The 66-year-old said his condition has been getting steadily worse, leading to him making one of his hardest decisions to quit the band.

The group, made up of Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes and guitarist John Taylor, said his decision came after "careful consideration and medical advice", which said that "protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first".

Taylor, who left the band in 1985 before returning in 2001, said: "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I'll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they've shown us over the years.

"But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse," he said.
