TechnologyTab.title: Global Microsoft outage affecting tens of thousands of users
TechnologyTab.text:
Microsoft is struggling to fix a major global outageof its service that is reportedly affecting tens of thousands of users.

Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot have been affected by "connectivity problems".

The company said in a series of updates on X that it was seeing "positive results" with its efforts to restore services and that it was rushing to fix the problem.

Reports of issues with Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector. The BBC understands there is no indication the outage was caused by a cyber-attack.

The disruption affects programs that are part of Microsoft 365 - a popular online service among businesses that allows them to use workplace tools like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive.

For international organisations, this platform is essential for connecting and collaborating with colleagues around the world.

Among the issues, users may be unable to view certain files or details on their calendar apps, Microsoft said.

Its AI platform, Copilot, may also be unable to work properly.

Messaging and online meetings were largely functional, the firm added.

Microsoft said on X that the outage was caused by a number of servers "being unexpectedly unavailable", straining its remaining systems.

"We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible," said a Microsoft spokesperson.

The company later warned that some services that had been restored "can become unresponsive again", adding that customers "in any region" could be affected.

Users around the world including the US, Japan and Singapore have reported facing disruptions.

TechnologyTab.title: Firm offers to fake artworks for wealthy migrants seeking UK 'talent' visas - BBC investigation
TechnologyTab.text:
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.

The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.

Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.

We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.

No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.

In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.

A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.

"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.

The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.

A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".

They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:

At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying

The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application

For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.

The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.

A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".

Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".

The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.

About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.

The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.

Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".

Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.

"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.

Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.

Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.

During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.

The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.

It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.

Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.

This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.

Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.

The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.

The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.

During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.

The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.

"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."

He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".

When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.

"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".

"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."

The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".

Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.

The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.

The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".

It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.

Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.

"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."

Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.

Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.

The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.

Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.

If you would like to contact our team about this story you can email on: politicsinvestigations@bbc.co.uk, external

EntertainmentTab.title: Eurovision Song Contest is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up in Thailand
EntertainmentTab.text:
On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.

And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.

It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.

Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.

"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.

"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.

"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.

This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.

Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.

Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.

There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.

A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.

Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.

The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.

Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.

The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".

In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.

Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.

For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.

"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."

Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988.

Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets.

Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest.

EntertainmentTab.title: Timothée Chalamet among Hollywood stars and charity heroes stepping up for BBC Children In Need
EntertainmentTab.text:
Timothée Chalamet and his Dune co-stars will be seen pranking Rylan Clark during this year's Children in Need on Friday.

The Oscar-nominated actor will be seen making the presenter sweat with suggestions from children behind-the-scenes in an Impractical Jokers-style set-up, during an interview with Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy about the third installment of the film franchise.

This year's Children in Need show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Last year's appeal raised more than £45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.

The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They will welcome Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.

Wyn Evans completed his 400-mile four-nation cycle ride through England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and his native Wales - finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

He raised more than £3.8m along the way.

EntertainmentTab.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
EntertainmentTab.text:
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.

The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.

La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."

The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."

Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.

She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.

The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.

He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.

Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.

Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".

"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.

She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.

Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".

EntertainmentTab.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says US move humbled her before big break with Steven Spielberg
EntertainmentTab.text:
Catherine Zeta-Jones has said she had an ego check after moving to America in the 1990s.

The Swansea-born star had become a household name in the UK, but Hollywood quickly provided a reality check for the rising star and she was even asked by casting agents if she had any acting experience.

It was during her stint on CBS mini-series Titanic that she was seen by Steven Spielberg who suggested she go for a role in The Mask of Zorro which he was producing.

"Five days later I got the job, and three days after that, I was down there starting my sword-fighting lessons," she said.

Zeta-Jones had become a star in the UK thanks to her breakout role in The Darling Buds of May that originally aired from 1991 to 1993.

But when she touched down in California, she was no longer recognised by the public and had a six-month visa to "give America a shot".

But Zeta-Jones told Business Insider it was "good" for her to have her ego knocked down a bit.

It was only when the Spielberg saw the Titanic series that she was given a major opportunity.

"I was shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas," she said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Download 2027 line-up: Blink-182 to headline on festival debut
EntertainmentTab.text:
Blink-182, Evanescence & Bring Me The Horizon have been announced as headliners of next year's Download Festival.

The trio are among more than 100 rock and metal acts set to play the event at Donington Park, Leicestershire from 9 to 13 June.

Other acts on the bill include The Prodigy, 5 Seconds of Summer and a special performance by heavy metal legends Mötley Crüe.

US pop-punk band Blink-182 will be making their Download debut, while Evanescence will become the festival's second female-fronted headliner.

The American rock band were founded by singer Amy Lee in the mid-1990s and had a UK number one with their best-known single Bring Me to Life in 2003.

It's the second year in a row a female-led band has headlined the festival, after Linkin Park topped the bill in 2025.

The nu-metal group have reformed with Emily Armstrong as their lead singer, after the death of former frontman Chester Bennington, who took his own life in 2017.

The choice of Emily upset some fans, who pointed to her alleged ties to the Church of Scientology and past support for convicted rapist Danny Masterson - someone she distanced herself from.

Next year's Download will be a first for Blink-182, who emerged from the California skate punk scene in the 1990s.

They've had two UK top 10 singles and had their first number one album in 2016, 21 years after their first record.

Their drummer Travis Barker is married to Kourtney Kardashian and survived a plane crash in the US that killed four people in 2008.

British rockers Bring Me The Horizon are more familiar to Download regulars, headlining for the second time in five years.

The four-piece band, formed in Sheffield, announced earlier this year they're celebrating 20 years of the debut album Count Your Blessings by re-recording it.

That 2006 record was in the deathcore genre, known for its heavy and aggressive sound, but the band have since moved towards metalcore, pop and electronic rock.

Some fans questioned if the original lyrics, which frontman Oli Sykes admitted could be interpreted as misogynistic, were still appropriate.

But the 39-year-old lead vocalist told the BBC Radio 1 Rock Show that going back to their roots was "a lot of fun" as they "got to remake the album how we wanted it to sound back then".

EntertainmentTab.title: Duran Duran's Roger Taylor quits Birmingham band over tinnitus
EntertainmentTab.text:
Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor said he will leave the band due to his worsening tinnitus.

Taylor has been the chart-topping group's drummer since they formed in Birmingham in 1978, which he described as "the joy of my life", but said he had "reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors".

The 66-year-old said his condition has been getting steadily worse, leading to him making one of his hardest decisions to quit the band.

The group, made up of Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes and guitarist John Taylor, said his decision came after "careful consideration and medical advice", which said that "protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first".

Taylor, who left the band in 1985 before returning in 2001, said: "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I'll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they've shown us over the years.

"But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: King Charles appears on Sir Elton John's radio show
EntertainmentTab.text:
King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

During the Rocket Hour show, the King said the pop star had become "a national treasure after all these years", to which the singer joked: "I'll be on the Antiques Roadshow."

"Join the club," the King replied.

The pair discussed some of their favourite musical performances, as well as the role music has played in the King's charity, the King's Trust. The show was recorded in secret last month and will air this Saturday.

Sir Elton has long been a supporter of the trust, most recently donating a pair of his rose-tinted glasses to its 50th anniversary auction this year.

In a trailer for the upcoming episode, the King and Sir Elton are seen laughing together as they chat.

In a voiceover, the singer said he was "excited to hear what he's got to say about music, about the King's Trust and memories that we both share".

The King's Trust - previously known as The Prince's Trust - was established by Charles in 1976 to help young people from disadvantaged backgrounds overcome challenging situations, become employed or launch their own businesses.

During the radio episode, the King called it "an opportunity too good to resist" when he was asked to showcase music from the "talented performers who have so generously supported us over the years, together with some of the newer artists the trust has helped to launch".

The full list of their chosen tracks is under wraps until the episode airs but Skye Newman's Hairdresser, Raye's Joy and Muse's rendition of Feeling Good are said to be among them.

The pair will reminisce about some of the most memorable performances for the trust, from the Wembley Arena rock galas of the 1980s - which Sir Elton participated in - to charity shows at the Royal Albert Hall and pop concerts in Hyde Park.

The episode was recorded at Apple Music Studios - which hosts the show - in Battersea Power Station when the King and Sir Elton visited for the launch of the Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs.

The mentorship programme aims to help young people explore careers in creative industries.

EntertainmentTab.title: Julia Garner Would Rather Be Someone Else
EntertainmentTab.text:
Julia Garner doesn’t like to think of what she does as acting, not once the cameras are rolling. “I’m just being at that moment,” she said. “I’m just living it.”

She knows how that sounds. “Super artsy,” she said. “Actory.” She can’t help it. “I always want to act and feel like no one is watching me,” she said.

In life, Garner, 32, doesn’t hide. I’d met up with her at Zitomer’s, a multilevel pharmacy on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. This was Garner’s suggestion. She’s been a regular since her high school days, and the salesladies swarmed her. “Hi, honey!” one cooed as Garner swept in.

Garner, pointed out a peel she loves, the first grown-up lipstick she bought, then moved onto blinged-out pill cases, bed jackets and furry Russian hats.

She insisted that I try out a moisturizer with the horrifying name of CelluMoist, and because Garner is sweetly indomitable, I submitted, letting a clerk slather it on. Minutes later I had to wrestle a makeup bag out of Garner’s hand, explaining that our ethics policy prevented her buying it for me. I won. Barely. To be around her, at least on that late summer afternoon, was to be swept up in a very benevolent whirlwind — a twister of zip and warmth and sharp acuity.

I hadn’t expected this. Though Garner’s body of work (“The Americans,” “Ozark,” “The Assistant,” “Weapons”) is unusually varied, none of it implies that she would be a fun hang. But Garner is a transformational actress. By method and by choice she is nothing like the characters she plays.

“When somebody comes along like Julia, who’s beautiful and talented and daring in the way that she is, it feels important,” said Zach Cregger, who directed her in “Weapons,” the buzzy 2025 horror hit. “She just throws herself into all these different roles and is unrecognizable.”

Even out of roles, Garner doesn’t always recognize herself. To me, she seemed distinct, delightfully sui generis. But maybe that was only the Julia of that day, that hour.

Her latest transformation is in “The Altruists,” a Netflix limited series that premieres on Nov. 19. Created by Graham Moore, “The Altruists” describes the spectacular rise and precipitous fall of FTX and Alameda Research, cryptocurrency concerns founded by Sam Bankman-Fried. Garner plays Caroline Ellison, the chief executive of Alameda Research and Bankman-Fried’s off-again-on-again romantic partner. Their relationship — amatory, professional — is depicted as a blockchain folie à deux that ends with both of them imprisoned for crimes including fraud and conspiracy.

You would not think that a person like Garner could disguise her looks easily. With her milky skin, sharp chin, liquid eyes and meringue-like blond curls, she has a delicate, distinct elegance. But the first time Anthony Boyle, who plays Bankman-Fried, saw her fully made up, he mistook her for a background actor.

“It was like a magic trick,” he said. “She was a different person.”

That magic, that sense of not acting but being, is the goal. “I like to become different people,” Garner said. “I am really just trying to completely disappear.”

Early on, she went out for teen and tween parts on Nickelodeon series, but she did not get them. Her look and affect were better suited to indies. She had a significant role in the 2011 cult drama “Martha Marcy May Marlene” and a starring one in “Electrick Children,” a coming-of-age film from 2012. Studio executives encouraged her to dye her hair and get veneers, but she resisted.

“I was like, they have no taste,” she recalled.

She entered the mature phase of her career a few years later on the FX series “The Americans,” playing an C.I.A. officer’s daughter, and was a standout on the Netflix rural crime show “Ozark,” as a baby-faced, dirty-mouthed criminal matriarch.

In these roles and elsewhere, there was a sense of risk in her performances, a heightened emotional intensity or an uncanny remove. Garner described herself as drawn to extremes.

“If I read something and I’m not scared to do it, I just don’t do it,” she said.

She also lends her characters a sense of unpredictability, an aliveness, which she ascribes in part to her experience of childhood epilepsy, never knowing when the next seizure would come. “There is something about that that forces you to be present,” she said.

Garner has an unusual approach to acting. When preparing a role, she invites a character in. “I literally can physically feel when I’m leaving and having another person coming,” she said. “It sounds so crazy.”

The character of Caroline came in from pretty far away. Ellison was a math prodigy; Garner failed math. Ellison is emotionally illiterate; Garner is an emotional whiz. They look nothing alike. But Garner saw “The Altruists” as an opportunity for complete transformation.

“I just wanted to see how far I could go,” she said.

This was why Moore wanted her, too. “Julia is such a high diver,” he said. “She will choose to jump from the highest platform into the deepest water.” Even he was surprised at Garner’s push for physical transformation — colored contacts, facial prosthetics, a wig system, which meant more than two hours each day in the makeup trailer.

Unlike Anna Sorokin, whom Garner played in the Netflix series “Inventing Anna,” Ellison declined a request to meet. From the few videos of her available, Garner roughed out a gawky walk and a gasping laugh. She moved her voice to a lower register, frayed at the ends, and accelerated her speech.

Boyle, acting opposite her, admired her ability to combine this immersion in the role with the practicality a shoot demands. “She treads that line of being able to call on genius and be possessed by it at will and also be in reality,” he said.

“I have to make sure to feed my soul, as corny as that sounds,” she said. “Feed my soul as a human. Because I don’t play actresses, I play people.”

I realized only later, playing back the interview, that she had said almost nothing about that offscreen human. She hadn’t seemed evasive at the time. (Of her separation from her husband, the musician Mark Foster, she said simply, “There’s nothing really to talk about.”) And yet her most personal details were about moisturizer. Just now she seems to live for her work. And there’s plenty of it.

She has recently finished filming “Tyrant,” a suspense movie set in the world of fine dining, co-starring Charlize Theron. Garner will next play one half of an adulterous couple in another thriller, “Guilty Creatures.” She has also shot an episode of the Apple TV Hollywood satire “The Studio,” in which she plays “a crazy version of myself,” opposite Madonna. (Garner was cast as Madonna in a biopic, which remains mired in development.)

I was reminded of something Moore had said, that if you tried to draw a through line linking Garner’s various roles, you would end up with a series of cartoon squiggles. But “The Studio” aside, she has almost never played a character who is happy or at ease or has even half the exuberance and impishness that she displayed that afternoon.

EntertainmentTab.title: How Peter Farrelly Captured a New Side of ‘Rocky’
EntertainmentTab.text:
In “Anatomy of a Scene,” we ask directors to reveal the secrets that go into making key scenes in their movies. See new episodes in the series on Fridays. You can also watch our collection of more than 350 videos on YouTube and subscribe to our YouTube channel.

The movie “I Play Rocky" charts the long and obstacle-hurtling path that Sylvester Stallone took to getting the movie “Rocky” to the big screen. Directed by Peter Farrelly, the movie structures its making-of-“Rocky” narrative in the same triumphant underdog way that the director of “Rocky” structured the original.

This sequence takes place during the shooting of a dramatic sequence in “Rocky.” Anthony Ippolito portrays Sylvester Stallone as he is playing Rocky. And Robert Morgan portrays Burgess Meredith as he is playing Mickey, a trainer, former boxer and the owner of the gym Rocky frequents. In the sequence, after Rocky has been picked to face the heavyweight champion of the world, Apollo Creed, for a chance at the title, Mickey offers to be Rocky’s manager. But Rocky sends him away because he believes Mickey never cared about his potential during the many years he’d been training there.

But in the scene as originally written, Rocky immediately chases after Mickey, without a sense of what might have motivated him to do so. During the shoot, the director of “Rocky,” John G. Avildsen (played by Jay Duplass), feels that the scene is not making sense because he doesn’t understand why Rocky would go after Mickey when Mickey has been critical of Rocky’s talent until now. He challenges Stallone to devise a way to make the sequence come together emotionally.

Stallone takes a break and has a conversation with his wife, Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb). She pushes him to think about why he wrote the scene, and who in his real life never gave him a chance to succeed. With his dismissive father in his head, Stallone returns to the set to shoot the scene, ad-libbing a monologue that feels like an outpouring of his anger over how he’s been treated.

It’s not a scene that most people discuss when talking about “Rocky” (the training montage is usually at the top of the list), but in an interview, Farrelly said, “This is gonna be the scene that people most remember in ‘I Play Rocky.’”

It’s a turning point in the movie, one that zeros in on the many obstructions that have impeded Stallone as he is trying to star in his first movie, the studio skeptical that he will be able to make it work, or that his performance will be up to par. But he transcends those negative thoughts in this moment, wowing both his director and his producers on the set.

EntertainmentTab.title: Offset Is Tired of Being Rap’s Bad Guy: ‘I Got Lost’
EntertainmentTab.text:
Modern rap stardom can be both musical and extramusical. Offset, who came to fame as a member of the superstar Atlanta rap trio Migos, alongside Quavo and Takeoff, has had a heavy dose of each.

Born Kiari Cephus, Offset, 34, was one of the artists who remade the sound of hip-hop at the dawn of streaming in the 2010s, helping cement Atlanta as a center of rap innovation and success. Following the group’s early hits like “Versace” and “Fight Night,” which established their trademark flow through percussive repetition, Offset differentiated himself by writing the hook for “Bad and Boujee,” one of the decade’s defining rap songs and an unlikely Billboard No. 1.

But he was also the Migos member with the most fraught personal life: As the trio celebrated early triumphs, he was in and out of jail, facing a tangle of charges stemming from a youthful conviction for burglary.

Over the last few years, Offset has become as visible for his personal foibles and setbacks as his musicmaking. His marriage to, and split from, Cardi B provided years of tabloid fodder, making him a regular and reliable villain of the social internet. Earlier this year, he was shot outside a Florida casino. And he’s still living under the long shadow cast by the 2022 fatal shooting of Takeoff — a close friend from adolescence whom he continues to refer to as a brother — which occurred while Offset was suing Migos’s label and estranged from the group.

JOE COSCARELLI Let’s start with the title track, “GMFU.” This is the place you put years of angst, everything you’ve been through recently — Takeoff’s death, your own shooting, your marriage collapsing. What was your mind-set going into recording a clearing-the-air song, and how does it differ from the mind-set that you’re in now?

OFFSET I got lost. I went through so many hits, and I feel like it became a blur to what my passion is, which is music, you know? The personal takes went so far on things that have happened in my life that I’ve taken full accountability of before, and it’s like, sometimes I can’t escape the matrix of this narrative. And so when I made this album, I got in a bag where I was like, you know what, I’m going to just focus on this music. I don’t really hear all the noise. I am a great person. I know this. I have Black women around me that know I’m a great man at the end of the day: my mother, my creative director-slash-manager. And I got children that I look out for, that I’m a great father to. And sometimes other things blur that, and it bothers me.

Because you got to understand, when I first started, I was the knucklehead in the group. I was going to jail. I ain’t been to jail in over 10 years. I straightened that, and it was so hard to stray from that to become a professional. And to grow up. My music is my pulse, my heart. That’s all I have. And so I wasn’t treating it that way, because of all the other things that was happening. I went into the dark space, gambling. When I gambled, it’s just like, OK, this is just about this — I don’t have to see no tabloids or worry about somebody saying something about me. It blinds you as if it’s not an issue, and it really is an issue.

COSCARELLI This villain narrative out there — is it because of your personal life?

OFFSET Yeah, it’s the past relationship. What’s so crazy is we good — me and her good. It was a patch of time that happened. We have children. We see the bigger thing. Me and her cool. But it’s more the people, you know what I’m saying, more than what’s actually happened in real life. Like, I have no issues with my ex. I salute everything that she’s doing.

JON CARAMANICA But that doesn’t travel as well on the internet as when you’re not good. People are obviously going to amplify the negative. Are you trying to be proactive to demonstrate that things are good now?

CARAMANICA Do you think that the things that people get frustrated with or talk about online — your villain narrative — are the same things that you experienced as you were lost, or is it two totally separate things?

OFFSET Uhhhh, they go together, ’cause I was doing lost [expletive], publicly. So it’s kind of on me. It’s not kind of — it’s on me.

COSCARELLI Was there any side of you that was like, you know what, they have a point?

OFFSET A million percent. Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

CARAMANICA Was that hard to look at — like, these are strangers on the internet, and they can see that I’m not doing right?

OFFSET It wasn’t so tough when you’ve got a strong mama who’s going to tell you what it is.

Sometimes it takes for somebody at home to shake you up, like, hey, what you doing? And then I can sometimes see the hurt in my mama. And that burns my soul, bro. Burns my soul. I’ve been trying to change for my family’s sake, and then sometimes it don’t go nowhere. I don’t know what to do a lot of times, but I do have to acknowledge that I brought all this [expletive] on myself. I went through dark times.

COSCARELLI Your marriage is imploding.

OFFSET My brother died.

COSCARELLI Takeoff died, of course, in this same stretch. And then you have this incident at a casino. You got shot. There’s these photos of you in the hospital — you’re smoking a cigarette in a wheelchair, and your mom is with you. She looks like she’s —

OFFSET She’s getting on my ass. She ain’t playing, because I broke my mama’s heart, bro. I ain’t never seen my mama like that.

COSCARELLI Even with all you’ve been through?

OFFSET All I’ve been through, that was a different moment. Like, my mama eyes — like, her baby boy. You know, when I got hit, I called my mama, so she wouldn’t hear it from the street. You know, “I’m good, I just got to go to the hospital” — hung up. Actually, my phone died, which was worse. She flew in so fast. When I was outside, I’m talking to her — really, I wanted to get up out of there — but she gave it to me: You being a coward to your kids by making choices like this that’s affecting everybody. You could be dead. You know, she gave me the talk. You the savior to the family. What you doing? But it wasn’t that nice, you know what I mean? It wasn’t nice. My mama hold me accountable. She’s worried, but it was more like, you need discipline.

COSCARELLI How do you start to build yourself back up?

OFFSET When I was saying lost, I was not moving as Offset, because I didn’t want to be Offset at one point. Because it was just too much. It’s like, working hard to become an artist, and then your relationship smokes that whole [expletive]. And I ain’t playing no victim, though. I don’t want to play no victim. I don’t want people to see this and be like, are you playing a victim? I’m just saying, I’m tired of that.

COSCARELLI What did you have to change lifestyle-wise, post-shooting, to make sure you could be Offset again?

OFFSET At that time, I wasn’t even recording. I was literally trying to get away from folks. I wasn’t trying to go to no club, no strip club. I just was sitting around. I just want to be Kiari. I was trying to get back to the person, to be present. Because the opposite person ain’t working.

COSCARELLI Do you feel like you have a problem with gambling?

OFFSET I don’t know. I’m going to be a million percent real with y’all. I like to gamble, right? I feel like I need to stop. I need to stop. But I feel like a problem is when you, like, selling [expletive], you ain’t got the money to do it. I’m doing this [expletive] to get away. And I do like to gamble, to be honest. A lot of plays I get, you think I’m gambling, and I’ve been paid a lot of money to maybe promote it.

CARAMANICA Like from gambling platforms?

OFFSET Yeah, so I might have a sponsorship from them. They have a lot of budget. Sometimes you think I’m gambling and I might’ve collabed with somebody, but I just made $400,000 doing this. I’ma keep it real, like — I can say I got a problem. I’m not trying to give myself an excuse, because I sound kind of excuse-y.

CARAMANICA All this music on the new album was recorded after the shooting?

OFFSET All after. Yeah. I went right to the lab. I got out of the hospital, I’m in the studio.

COSCARELLI I remember the same thing happened when you almost died in a car wreck.

OFFSET You make the smashes when you go through stuff and go straight to the studio, ’cause now you got something to talk about. And I started just talking like that. It put me back in the focus mind. And I’m just being honest, you got to distract yourself from that. Because it’s a deep tunnel going into that, and you can’t come back sometimes, you feel me? So I just got to work.

OFFSET I don’t look at it like that. For me, it’s like, I know I’m not Migos. That’s three monsters in one machine, right? So it’s not a frustration for me, it’s a building for me. I got four solo albums out, right? Every album, I caught a single that went to Billboard, right? So I never did a flop album, in my eyes.

Might not have been as peak as Migos, but Migos took 15 years to get to that peak. Y’all just seen it after five or six — we’ve been rappers since eighth grade. So I still remember that it’s a buildup. I feel like a lot of people really get lost in the sauce when they don’t recognize things are changing, bro. You still could be a big artist and in a good position, still make millions every year, but you’re not recognizing the change.

EntertainmentTab.title: Can Music Build Empathy? Silkroad’s Mission Is to Prove It Can
EntertainmentTab.text:
When the cellist Yo-Yo Ma started a global music collective in 2000, the world was a very different place. It was before 9/11, before immigration policy re-emerged as core political issue and before foreign performers became routinely shut out of touring in the United States because of visa blocks and skyrocketing fees.

Back then, Ma’s idea was to celebrate the multiplicity of musical styles and cultures along the ancient Silk Road, which stretched from East Asia to the Mediterranean. As the Silk Road Ensemble, the musicians championed artistic connection as a vehicle for building empathy.

These days, the organization operates as Silkroad, with the manifoldly talented musician Rhiannon Giddens as its artistic director. Now, the project is far less tidily summed up, and even more sprawling. There’s the ensemble, a bunch of variously sized touring groups, with 36 members on the roster; a Global Music Workshop in Boston and Hangzhou, China, which puts musicians into cross-cultural collaborations; outreach efforts bringing Silkroad performers into underserved and marginalized communities; and an array of educational programs, as well as recordings, a documentary film and a podcast.

Silkroad is celebrating its 25th anniversary this Saturday evening with a gala concert at Carnegie Hall, featuring both Ma and Giddens as well as a host of other Silkroad artists from across the globe.

Ma pointed to “Wedding,” a piece by the Syrian-born composer and clarinetist Kinan Azmeh. “Before we played it,” Ma said, “Kinan would say: ‘This piece is inspired by all the joy of a Syrian village wedding, and it reminds us that falling in love is a human right that can never be taken away.’ I think that moment and sentiment contain the heart of what Silkroad stands for — culture’s power to remind us of our essential humanity, even in the face of fracture and pain and destruction.”

Giddens, who became artistic director in 2020, noted that societal fissure and isolation became more acute during the pandemic, which emerged just as she was figuring out how she wanted to lead this already mature organization. “As in: ‘How can I be useful? What is the thing that I bring that nobody else can bring?’” she said.

Giddens realized her foundation in improvisational music could provide a new axis. There were plenty of Silkroad artists who came out of improvisatory traditions, but the group was rooted in Western classical music. That meant its core efforts hewed to the classical model: creating and then performing written compositions in big concert halls.

“I said, ‘That’s great,” Giddens said, “‘but we’ve been doing that for 20 years.’ We’ve been asking these folks from these different non-Western traditions to meet us in a certain way. Can we not go over a little bit to their side?”

That shift, Giddens said, also led Silkroad to its latest project, “Sanctuary,” which explores music’s capacity to provide refuge and navigate uncertainty. And it has transformed how Silkroad tours.

“Instead of going show to show,” Giddens said, “we go into a community for three days. Ideally, we’ll have two days of different kinds of community engagements, and then the third day will be the concert,” for which Silkroad provides tickets to community participants.

“This year,” Hartley said, “we had musicians come off tour saying, ‘This is the best tour I’ve ever done.’ We said, ‘Did you say the best Silkroad tour?’ They said, ‘No. The best tour I’ve ever done.’”

The Scottish-born harpist and composer Maeve Gilchrist recalled a performance she and the Moroccan guimbri player Mehdi Nassouli gave in June for preschoolers in Oklahoma.

“I have a 3-year-old, and I’ve never seen her sit as still as these kids,” Gilchrist said. “We offered them the chance to play the harp. We had a line of about 40 kids, and we stayed for every one of them.”

Silkroad musicians say these experiences have transformed their lives.

“If I hadn’t joined Silkroad, if I hadn’t met Yo-Yo, I probably would just be someone who’s good at his art,” said Sandeep Das, an Indian tabla player and composer who has been part of the collective since its early days. “The biggest journey has been from being just a good musician into learning the importance of being a good human being first.”

Just as Ma and his collaborators envisioned all those years ago.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Lincoln in the Bardo’ Pulls the Metropolitan Opera Into the YouTube Era
EntertainmentTab.text:
Lifted by celebrity endorsements, strong social media interest and favorable reviews, the Metropolitan Opera’s world premiere of “Lincoln in the Bardo” quickly sold out all nine of its performances this fall.

It is an unusually strong showing by a new opera, even one based on a book as popular as George Saunders’s 2017 novel, and it presented a quandary for the Metropolitan Opera. Given the inflexibility of its long-planned season schedule — not to mention the schedules of its sprawling, starry cast — the Met couldn’t simply pop a few more performances on the calendar. And Met executives had not included “Lincoln” on its roster of performances to be simulcast to 1,900 cinemas in 53 countries as part of its Live in HD series.

A solution was found. The final performance of “Lincoln,” on Saturday, will be livestreamed on the Met’s YouTube channel, which has 336,000 subscribers and is typically used for promotion. (It will be available through Nov. 18.) This is the first time the Met has streamed an entire opera on YouTube, a move that could potentially transform the way its productions are made available to a wider audience, particularly new operagoers and those who do not live in New York.

Paul Cremo, the director of the Met’s opera commissioning program, said: “We are really excited that people are getting to see it for free across the country and around the world, as well as people who wanted to see it again and couldn’t get tickets. There’s a lot of interest in it.”

But since the Met’s YouTube channel is free, there will be no revenue for the financially struggling company. The last time the Met streamed performances was during the pandemic, when it posted archive Live in HD recordings on its website. The Met sells an average of 100,000 tickets for Live in HD broadcasts, which produced $3 million in revenue in the 2024-25 season, said Gillian Brierley, the Met’s assistant general manager for marketing and communications.

Nevertheless, the Met is using the YouTube stream as a tool in its $1.5 billion fund-raising campaign: an onscreen fund-raising appeal allowing viewers to make contributions, starting at $1. (Viewers can disable the fund-raising button.)

“This is unknown territory,” Gelb said. “We haven’t done something quite as populist, in terms of free programming to a mass audience, since the pandemic. I don’t know how many people will watch it.”

Given the intimate nature of the small screen, some accommodations had to be made. A dummy used to depict Willie Lincoln in his coffin needed to be more lifelike for the cameras, so the Met made lifelike rubber casts of the head and hands of Everett Sobers, the 12-year-old singer who depicts Willie.

The success of “Lincoln,” with a score by Missy Mazzoli and a libretto by Royce Vavrek, comes as the Met has sought to add new works to a repertoire once dominated by traditional opera. Since the pandemic, it has presented 17 operas by living composers, including two world premieres: the staged version of Kevin Puts’s “The Hours,” and “Lincoln.”

“The audience has changed,” Cremo said. “I have been here 21 years. I have seen a real sea change in the sea of white-haired heads out in the audience. And there are a lot of young people who have grown up on cool indie films and TV. They are narratively very sophisticated. They are interested in diversity. And they want to see a world that reflects the world that they are living in.”

On average, new operas have sold about 10 percent more seats per performance than works from the traditional repertory. Some new operas have sold particularly well, among them Mason Bates’s “The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay” and Gabriela Lena Frank’s “El Último Sueño de Frida y Diego.” Others — including Kaija Saariaho’s “Innocence” and Jeanine Tesori’s “Grounded” — have been less successful.

GeneralTab.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
GeneralTab.text:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

GeneralTab.title: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of Birmingham knife attack
GeneralTab.text:
A former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.

Mohammed Alfatih, previously known as Mohammed Naim, was regularly seen acting as a bodyguard for a former leader of Hamas in 2006. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.

The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawfully wounding a bailiff who had come to repossess his wife's car, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of wounding with intent.

Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terror unit at the moment he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year.

The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not be named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.

During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath and trying to stab the bailiff as he drove away.

He told the court he chased the victim across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts of more than £2,250 linked to unpaid parking fines.

Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.

Jurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group Hamas or his work as a bodyguard to its now-deceased former leader Ismail Haniyeh.

But it can now be revealed that while detained for the attack in Birmingham, he was re-arrested when authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged gun plot to attack Jewish targets there.

It is alleged Alfatih was an organiser and was involved in the movement of weapons.

German authorities also allege he had pre-recorded a video wearing a balaclava and sunglasses claiming the attack was planned on behalf of the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas. The alleged attack was prevented after a tip-off from the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad.

Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK.

During his evidence, Alfatih did not mention Hamas but told the court he had been tortured for 25 days while detained in Egypt in 2010.

The father-of-four, an IT worker, failed in a legal application to try to get the wounding charges thrown out on the grounds of prejudicial media coverage about the investigation in Germany.

During the two-week trial at Birmingham Crown Court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.

Bailiff Kevin Bucknall was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment, but the defendant had pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.

Alfatih told jurors it had happened a day after he had learned one of his brothers had been killed in Gaza.

He also said while giving evidence that traumatic experiences in his past included being shot and injured on two different occasions.

The BBC understands that when Alfatih went by the name of Naim, he enrolled in a VIP protection course and was selected to accompany Haniyeh on trips to Egypt and other countries between 2006 and 2008. However, he was later removed from the role due to his behaviour.

The second son of former Hamas health minister Bassem Naim, he later spent time in Malaysia, Qatar and Turkey before arriving in Britain.

Following his conviction, a government source said it was "staggering" that he was granted asylum and later given citizenship.

A Home Office spokesperson added Hamas was a proscribed terrorist organisation and the government condemned "those who choose to support its activities and further its aims".

GeneralTab.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
GeneralTab.text:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Our proposals were almost laughed at.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

GeneralTab.title: Heat pumps: How much heat does your home really need?
GeneralTab.text:
Floorplans. Air duct diagrams. Heat pump specifications. Most people in the market for a new heating system probably don't want to think about this level of detail.

But, perhaps surprisingly, some do want to think about those things. In extreme depth.

Every day, roughly 150 new users sign up to an app called Cool Calc, which works out the heat requirements of properties in the US.

Just over one third of those new users are not tradespeople but private homeowners, says founder and chief executive Bill Fiore.

When choosing a heating system, people can find themselves bombarded with information – how powerful a heat pump do they need, for example? It isn't always easy to take a tradesperson at their word.

"As an overall trend, we are seeing homeowners be more informed," explains Fiore. "They want to do a calculation on their own."

A heat loss calculation is a figure, usually measured in watts, that defines how much heat a home loses during cold weather. It's worked out room by room and is a key part of designing an efficient heating system.

This estimate is especially important to get right when installing a heat pump, which is sized fairly precisely, according to the projected heat loss.

Should that calculation be off, the heat pump will likely perform poorly. You could be left with an underpowered device that struggles to warm your property, for example. Given the costs involved, homeowners are often anxious to ensure installers avoid such mistakes.

Certain new technologies are not, for the moment, helping, adds Fiore. "People are going to AI and they're getting a lot of misinformation because it's not backed by anything credible," he says. Cool Calc is planning to integrate with AI chatbots to try and improve the quality of the advice they spew out.

It is probably a good idea to be cautious about your new heating system's design, says Kevin Kircher at Purdue University. He and colleagues recently conducted a study, yet to be published, examining the heat loss calculations provided by tradespeople to roughly 75 US homeowners.

"We were surprised," says Kircher. "The heat loss calculations often led to overestimating the design heat loads by a factor of two or more." That would result in oversized systems that use much more power than necessary.

Not only that, some people reported charges of more than $1,000 (£745) – and in one case as much as $2,500 – just for a heat loss survey, adds Kircher.

Besides using excessive amounts of energy, an oversized heating system can also feel uncomfortable, says Dan Dempsey, a former senior engineering fellow for a major heating and cooling provider in the US.

Dempsey, who took part in Kircher and his colleagues' study, lives in Indiana. He says it is his retirement hobby to monitor the performance of heating and cooling systems in the homes of friends and family members, by analysing data from their smart thermostats.

"I spent five years manually downloading everything, every week," he says. He points out that oversized systems tend to cycle a lot, meaning they switch on and off again in quick succession.

This leads to discernible swings in temperature: rooms that fail to remain at their target temperature of, say, 20C, but rather fluctuate, which feels uncomfortable, says Dempsey.

For people seeking a better understanding of their home's heat loss, various free or partially free apps, including Cool Calc and AutoHVAC, are available. There are options for UK homeowners, too, such as web app Heatpunk.

Doing your own heat loss calculation may end up "over-intellectualising" things, says Adam Chapman, chief geek at heat pump training firm and installer network Heat Geek.

"I don't personally see what a homeowner would gain from it," he says. "We will guarantee the efficiency with way less radiators and pipework upgrades than any other system out there."

Chapman points out that only the most careful of surveys will capture a home's heat loss well.

He says it is common for Heat Geek installers to discover retrofitted windows that haven't been foam-insulated into their openings, leaving draughty gaps, or cavity walls that a homeowner thought had been insulated – but which were actually missed by the builder.

"It's stuff you can't see," he says. "What we actually need is home surveys that go and spot for these sorts of things."

GeneralTab.title: Andy Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
GeneralTab.text:
Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.

The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".

The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.

Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line.

"But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."

Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".

He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."

Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".

On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."

The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".
