articles.title: Wall Street Loses a Powerful Dealmaker After Nvidia’s CEO Is Ousted
articles.text:
With Jensen Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia, Wall Street has lost its most powerful and profitable dealmaker.

As Mr. Huang built Nvidia from a regional chipmaker into the world’s largest company, he dispensed with the usual careful, corporate hand-wringing. He personally directed splashy deals and complicated financing structures that pumped hundreds of billions of dollars into would-be competitors, suppliers and customers.

If that made him, in the public eye, a face of the global A.I. build out, on Wall Street he represented something else: manna. His deals produced billions of dollars in fees for banks, asset managers and advisers, and Nvidia was, up until this week, spending or promising money at a speed and magnitude of little precedence.

Now Wall Street bankers, traders and even some of Nvidia’s competitors are wondering and worrying about whether Mr. Huang’s departure will slow the breakneck pace of Nvidia’s investments.

Some say that the fundamentals of Nvidia’s power are still intact, like its extreme control of the global supply of chips, the A.I. boom’s scarcest resource, the company’s deep cash coffers and the Trump administration’s warm support for the industry’s regulatory agenda. But Mr. Huang was the leader who harnessed all of those assets into a deal-making machine.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I.,” said Michael Edwards, director of Forum Markets, an A.I.-focused merchant bank. “Imagine the Fed without a chairman.”

Mr. Huang’s financial footprint is stamped all over the A.I. movement.

He steered tens of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s cash into bankrolling smaller A.I. companies — including Anthropic and OpenAI, helping them boom into the two behemoths of the space.

In August, Nvidia agreed to spend as much as $105 billion to back a giant data center in Ohio that is being built by SoftBank Energy and will be leased to OpenAI. At the time, Nvidia said it would offer financial guarantees for other data centers.

Nvidia has also struck deals to buy or effectively buy smaller competitors. Late last year, it said it would spend roughly $20 billion to license the technology of the chip start-up Groq and hire its top executive. In September, the company said it would buy Hugging Face, a library of open artificial intelligence models, for $12.9 billion.

Deals like that are the lifeblood of the financial world, producing fees for bankers and lawyers who charge thousands of dollars per hour. And Nvidia was increasingly reloading to do even more; this summer, with the help of three big banks, it completed its first bond offering in five years.

In turn, Wall Street firms were so enthusiastic to ingratiate themselves with Mr. Huang and Nvidia because he could mobilize other firms to spend hundreds of billions of dollars too, or at least promise to.

In one illustrative deal, Mr. Huang rang up David M. Solomon, Goldman Sachs’ chief executive, and others, with the idea that the bank and rivals assemble a joint consortium to lend to companies in need of expensive chips. Not a dime had been raised and even some inside the companies were unaware of it, when Mr. Huang nonetheless corralled the firms’ top brass in August to appear on CNBC and announce a half-trillion dollar target. Wall Street’s titans said they would do practically anything to help Mr. Huang keep the money rolling into A.I.

“This is calling all precincts” is how Apollo’s president, Jim Zelter, repeatedly described the effort during the CNBC appearance.

That financing initiative is in flux, according to three people involved in it but were not permitted to discuss the matter publicly. No loans have closed, and at least one of the six lenders that had agreed to it was on Thursday discussing dropping out, one of the people said.

That effort was signature Mr. Huang who, at seemingly every opportunity and with showmanlike style, carried the banner against technological doomerism and fatalism, arguing to continue to ratchet up the staggering pace of A.I. investment, a trend that became perhaps the singular underpinning for the stock market and broader economy.

With his trademark leather jacket, Mr. Huang consistently positioned himself and Nvidia as the industry’s model citizen and defender of A.I.’s importance to national security and America’s future.

He wasn’t shy to boast to financiers about his company’s importance. In March, after his company reported a $43 billion quarterly profit, Mr. Huang told an audience at Morgan Stanley that it was “the best quarter of earnings in the history of earnings,” and then a moment later expanded the time frame to “the history of humanity.” It was a lot of money, but not a record.

During his second administration, President Trump welcomed Mr. Huang and his policies into the White House. The two men have become close allies and used that alliance to bolster their respective agendas.

Still, not all hope has been lost on Wall Street. While Mr. Huang’s departure has prompted a sell off in Nvidia’s stock, stripping more than $1.5 trillion from its valuation, bankers and investors said that would not necessarily have negative implications for the initial public offering of the A.I. giant Anthropic still on track for next week.

Investors, optimistic market watchers said, did not sell all artificial intelligence stocks this week. Instead, they appear to be looking to diversify their A.I. investments away from Nvidia, potentially freeing up hundreds of billions of dollars to invest in Anthropic’s I.P.O.

The banks representing Anthropic on its I.P.O. are poised to generate more than $500 million in fees from its $1 trillion-plus listing.

articles.title: Bessent Faults Commerce Dept. for Failing to Blacklist Megaspeed
articles.text:
Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, blamed the Commerce Department on Friday for the government’s failure to sanction the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, saying that other departments had pushed for the measure but that Commerce “has the pen.”

The Treasury, Defense and State Departments and the U.S. trade representative were all in favor of putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist called the entity list for months, but the Commerce Department is in charge of that authority, Mr. Bessent said on CNBC on Friday.

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said, adding, “Treasury and my deputy has been pushing for this for months at the deputies level.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” he said. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

Frustration is boiling over within the administration and on Capitol Hill about Megaspeed, the company led by a woman U.S. intelligence deemed to be an asset for the Chinese government.

The woman, Alice Huang, had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang. Mr. Huang resigned from his company on Thursday in the wake of revelations about that and another affair, sending the company’s stock price cratering.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with other officials in recent months over technology exports, which his department oversees. He has urged caution on sweeping export restrictions and recommended more surgical action, drawing accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that his department has become too cozy with Nvidia and Mr. Huang.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Mr. Bessent had confronted Mr. Lutnick last week over his handling of Megaspeed, demanding to know why the United States had not already banned sales of advanced A.I. chips to the firm. Mr. Lutnick said he would move quickly to put restrictions on Megaspeed in place, people briefed on the exchange said.

The move to blacklist Megaspeed had been discussed earlier at a meeting of the deputies of cabinet officials, where Jeffrey Kessler, an under secretary in the Commerce Department, deferred on taking action, saying that the decision was up to Mr. Lutnick, the people said.

A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department denied that the conversation between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick took place. She said that the decision about whether to add companies to the entity list was an administration-wide one. The Treasury Department did not comment.

Mr. Bessent questioned on Friday what Mr. Huang and Nvidia had known about Megaspeed’s business, and suggested that Nvidia should be held accountable if it did not have adequate oversight.

Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips to set up data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese clients, a legal loophole in U.S. export controls. Both the Trump administration and Congress have been weighing rules to crack down on that business. The government was also investigating Megaspeed for allegedly smuggling some Nvidia chips into China, in violation of U.S. law.

“There is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down,” Mr. Bessent said.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s Resignation From Nvidia Worries the A.I. Start-Up World
articles.text:
For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days.

The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power.

“As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023.

So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups.

Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. It more than doubled its start-up investments in six months.

Perhaps more critically, Nvidia has provided start-ups and small companies with access to A.I. chips that would have been difficult for them to obtain otherwise, offering $165 billion in lease guarantees and other backstops for cloud computing to start-ups and other companies, according to securities filings. The company has a venture capital arm and a program called Inception that provides tens of thousands of start-ups with training and guidance on how to access chips and computing power.

Mr. Huang has also been the industry’s most vocal advocate for “open source” and “open weight” technology, which makes underlying A.I. technology freely available for anyone to use, which benefits start-ups. Nvidia shelled out nearly $20 billion to buy two open source-focused companies in the last year.

Mr. Huang’s departure adds more uncertainty to an already jittery market. Investors fear A.I. is in a bubble that could burst. And the tech industry also faces potential regulation and a slowdown in data center construction ushered in by the results of the midterm elections. Nvidia controls the vast majority of the world’s market for the computer chips that A.I. companies need to build and service their technology.

The change in leadership could make it more difficult for smaller companies to access the chips and cloud computing power they need to compete against well-funded tech giants like Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft. More practically, it throws a number of investment deals Nvidia has in the works into limbo.

Mike Volpi, an investor at Hanabi Capital, a venture capital firm that backs A.I. companies, said he expected Nvidia to take a more conservative approach to backstopping so many smaller cloud companies.

“My expectation is that we will see some turbulence and some of Nvidia funds coming out of the market in the short term,” he said.

The A.I. industry relies so much on Nvidia that commentators have started to caution against the risks.

Speaking to a standing-room-only audience of software developers in San Francisco last month before Mr. Huang came under fire, Dylan Patel, who runs SemiAnalysis, an A.I. research firm, warned that struggling young data center companies were having no problem securing revenue guarantees from Nvidia. That allowed the companies to then take on debt they otherwise wouldn’t have gotten.

“This is sort of a quite a risky proposition,” Mr. Patel said. “We’ll see what ends up happening there.”

Mr. Huang’s pro-start-up stance has delivered cash windfalls to venture capital investors over the past year, especially with Nvidia’s purchases of start-ups. The company bought the technology and hired employees from chipmaker Groq for roughly $20 billion last December and the A.I. open-source platform Hugging Face for about $14 billion in September.

“Jensen Huang, we have yet to meet, but bravo!” Joseph T. Hasselmann, a start-up investor who backed Groq, wrote on LinkedIn after the deal was announced.

Samantha Lau, who manages a tech stock portfolio at AllianceBernstein, an investment firm, said Mr. Huang’s exit would probably eliminate a key source of financing for companies like the young data center firms that have been planning public offerings, and dampen overall market enthusiasm.

“The god of circular financing is going into hibernation,” she said, referring to the A.I. industry’s many interconnected deals.

articles.title: Fewer Fed Meetings Raise Stakes of Warsh’s Communications
articles.text:
When officials at the Federal Reserve meet next month to vote on interest rates, they will have only a partial snapshot of the economy in hand. Fresh inflation data comes out the day after policymakers finalize their rate decision, leaving them without insight into whether price pressures in November continued to accelerate or showed signs of easing.

This predicament underscores why officials at the central bank broadly appear on board with a plan hatched by Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, to reduce the number of meetings convened each year to vote on interest rates.

The changes will be ushered in gradually, beginning next fall. In a revised schedule released on Thursday, the Fed confirmed that its policymakers will meet eight times in 2027, but that the Oct. 25-26 gathering will be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.”

By 2028, there will be just six meetings accompanied by policy votes, with two others focused on strategy.

Meeting less frequently, and at more evenly spaced intervals, has the clear benefit of giving officials a more consistent flow of economic data to parse when they gather to debate their policy settings. But there are trade-offs that will put more onus on Mr. Warsh to communicate openly about how the Fed is approaching its rate decisions and its thinking about the outlook, something he has so far resisted even as the central bank has embarked on raising rates this year.

“The decision process is more important than the timing,” said Esther George, who served as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City from 2011 to 2023. “And this committee is struggling a bit with how to communicate what exactly they mean.”

Since taking over as chairman in May, Mr. Warsh has embraced a different communications style than his predecessors. He has been much more circumspect about what he is willing to share, keeping his views about the economy close to his chest, as well as anything related to the policy outlook. That has resulted in occasional public remarks and abridged news conferences.

In fact, one of his first acts as chairman was to overhaul the Fed’s policy statement that accompanies rate decisions. It now is significantly shorter and less detailed.

The void has been filled by Mr. Warsh’s colleagues, who have continued to vocalize their thinking about how the economy is faring; the extent of the inflation problem that the Fed is facing; and often very explicitly, what the central bank should do with rates to address it.

For William English, a former director of the Fed’s monetary affairs division who is now a professor at Yale University, Mr. Warsh’s communications style is a consequential one that will grow more pronounced as the Fed meets more sparingly.

“He’s giving up a fair amount by communicating as little as he seems to want to communicate, and I worry that’s really not helpful for the public’s understanding of what the committee is trying to achieve,” said Mr. English.

“If you had a committee that was meeting really often, then you don’t necessarily have to communicate as much, because you’re going to be taking another step or not taking another step very soon,” he added. “The longer the gap, the more communication does matter.”

At the turn of next year, for example, there will be a roughly two-month gap between policy votes. According to the new schedule, the Fed’s final gathering, typically scheduled for December, will be on Nov. 16-17, 2027. Officials would next meet Jan. 25-26, 2028, if the tentative schedule holds. Notably, the Fed’s rate moves in the last three years have mostly been in the final quarter of the year.

Fewer gatherings raise the prospects that the Fed will have to move in bigger increments than its typical quarter-point pace to play catch-up if the economic backdrop changes rapidly between rate decisions. It could also mean that impromptu meetings, which in the past have been reserved for crises, might happen more regularly.

Each of these dramatic steps could potentially create a lot of havoc for financial markets if not properly explained. Clearer communication could also help the Fed avoid taking them in the first place, said Donald Kohn, who served as vice-chair of the Fed from 2006 and 2010 when Mr. Warsh was a governor.

If the Fed provided guidance that it was worried about the inflation backdrop, for example, markets would begin to price in additional policy tightening if the data came in worse than expected. “But, if you’re not telling the markets about what you’re worried about and how you’re viewing things, they’re not going to have the ability to get out ahead of you,” said Mr. Kohn.

The meeting schedule is just one facet of a broader overhaul that Mr. Warsh wants in how the Fed communicates. One of five task forces he formed is looking at the range of tools at the central bank’s disposal: from the release of quarterly economic projections by officials known as the “dot plot,” which Mr. Warsh has openly criticized, to the post-policy meeting news conferences and minutes that are released three weeks later.

Kurt Lewis, a former senior Fed adviser who is now head of central bank policy at the investment bank Piper Sandler, said he expects sweeping changes to the dot plot. He anticipates that it could be replaced by some form of an economic forecast, potentially provided by Fed staff instead of policymakers.

Changes to the dot plot would likely require the support of Mr. Warsh’s colleagues. But the chairman would have unilateral authority to decide how often he wants to hold news conferences, for example.

For Mr. Lewis, one thing is probably off limits no matter how much Mr. Warsh’s wants it to change: “No one is going to agree to talk less.”

articles.title: Deed Theft Is Rising, Along With Property Values
articles.text:
A dying woman with dementia. A doctor from Long Island. A couple renovating a home in Florida.

The three fell victim to a type of real estate fraud known as deed, or title, theft, in which someone forges documents or fakes an identity to take ownership of a home or vacant land. Criminals may impersonate the true owners and sell the property to unsuspecting buyers, or use it as collateral to obtain loans.

The rise in home property values, and, therefore, home equity, have made deed theft potentially lucrative, experts say. Homes owned by older people, homes that show signs of financial distress, and vacant homes or land may be especially vulnerable.

It’s not clear how common deed theft is nationally but awareness of the fraud is mounting, especially in the Northeast. Earlier this month, a Queens man became the first person convicted under a New York deed theft law passed in 2024. And New York City has created a special office of deed theft prevention to detect and investigate such fraud.

Reports of real estate crime in general rose by 32 percent in 2025, to more than 12,000 complaints, and associated financial losses rose to more than $275 million, according to the F.B.I.’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. The F.B.I. estimates it received 66 complaints about deed or title theft in 2025, representing $5.9 million in losses, compared with 75 complaints representing losses of almost $7 million from January through October of this year.

The National Association of Realtors surveyed real-estate executives nationally in 2025 and found that nearly two-thirds reported being aware of this type of fraud in their area within the past year, with awareness highest — 95 percent — in the Northeast.

But the fraud isn’t confined to one region. “It happens everywhere,” said Craig Haskins, president of the American Land Title Association, a trade group for title insurers and agents and real-estate closing professionals. The group’s survey this year of 245 title professionals in 40 states found that nearly three out of five had experienced at least one incident of attempted “seller impersonation” fraud, up from about a quarter two years earlier.

Here’s what to know about deed theft and related fraud.

How does deed theft work?

In a common scenario, thieves file a deed on a home or property to transfer ownership to themselves, often by forging the true owner’s signature or duping the owner into signing it.

In the recent case in Queens, a man pleaded guilty to stealing the home of an older woman with dementia in 2024 by forging her signature on a deed giving ownership of the home where she had lived for 40 years, and where she was receiving home care, to himself and an accomplice. The fake signature was also notarized with a forged signature. They next forged her signature on another deed transferring the home to his business, which he used to take out a $552,500 mortgage. He then paid off the owner’s mortgage and other liens, allowing him to steal the balance of more than $300,000 for his “personal benefit,” according to prosecutors.

The theft was discovered by the owner’s son and daughter-in-law when they opened suspicious mail at her home. As a result of the plea agreement, the home will be returned to the family of the woman, who died in 2025, according to the New York State attorney general’s office. (The accomplice’s trial is scheduled for early next year.)

What type of properties are most at risk?

That can vary. In New York City, complaints have been concentrated in Brooklyn and Queens, where criminals often target seniors and immigrants, and homes in historically Black neighborhoods. Deirdre Lok, director and managing attorney at the Weinberg Center for Elder Justice in Riverdale, N.Y., said someone who bought a brownstone in the 1970s or ’80s may not realize they own an asset now worth millions. (Clips from The New York Times show such homes could be purchased for $25,000 or $35,000, and sometimes even less.)

The situation can be complicated by “tangled title” properties, in which a home is passed down to heirs informally, with multiple people having ownership, or lacking clear documentation of ownership. That can make it difficult for owners to borrow against the home, and may make them more vulnerable to lowball offers from scammers, according to a study by New York University’s Furman Center.

In other areas, vacant land or unoccupied homes can be attractive to criminals because owners aren’t nearby to notice any changes or suspicious activity.

“Older people are more likely to own their own home and to have paid it off, and they are more likely to have a second home,” which may not be occupied year round, said Françoise Cleveland, government relations adviser with AARP.

Dreama Bilby, 77, and her husband, Larry, 79, said in an interview that they had moved out of their house in Tampa, Fla., years ago after a large tree fell on it. They relocated to an apartment, intending to eventually rebuild. But the Bilbys became worried when security cameras installed near the house spotted a man and woman they didn’t recognize stopping by the property. Their concern turned to alarm when the woman identified herself to a neighbor as the home’s new occupant. It turned out thieves had filed a fraudulent deed in February 2024, transferring ownership from the Bilbys. The thieves eventually pleaded guilty to criminal charges, according to the state attorney’s office in Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa.

“That was such a traumatic experience,” Ms. Bilby said in an interview. “It really did a number on me.”

In another vacant property case, a Long Island doctor was surprised when a neighbor reported in 2023 that a large home was being built on a wooded lot the doctor owned in Fairfield, Conn. It turned out that someone had used a forged power of attorney and fake documents in 2022 to fraudulently sell the land for $350,000 to an unsuspecting developer. A lawsuit filed in the case was settled in 2024.

How can I protect my property?

Many counties or local governments now offer free services that automatically notify property owners if any documents are filed related to their property. (The Bilbys said they were able to halt the transfer of the deed on their home before it became final, because they had signed up for alerts.)

If your county doesn’t offer electronic deed alerts, you can periodically check your property records. Most areas now offer online search tools.

If you are buying a home, consider purchasing owners’ title insurance, Mr. Haskins said. Lender title insurance protects the mortgage lender on a home purchase against any undiscovered liens on the property or gaps in the chain of ownership. Banks typically require it if you are financing the purchase of a home. But buyers can also ask about paying for optional coverage, either as an add-on or with a separate policy that protects them, including against fraud.

Be certain to specify what type of coverage you are seeking. Some policies provide protection only for fraud that occurred before the closing. Others can protect for fraud that occurs after you become the owner. Availability may vary by state.

Typically, owner premiums are charged as a one-time payment, based on a percentage of the home’s purchase price. Costs vary by state and by the home’s selling price. For example, Mr. Haskins said, an owner’s policy in Wisconsin on a home priced at $338,200, the state median, would be about $1,439, or 0.43 percent of the purchase price. In Florida, the cost for a home at the state median price of about $416,800 would be about $1,610, or about 0.39 percent.

Be cautious about commercial services that promise to “lock” the title to your property for a fee. The Federal Trade Commission has warned that “title lock” services are not insurance and essentially charge for alerts that government services offer free.

Other tips: Pay close attention to your mail and email. If you stop receiving regular tax and utility bills or get bills that seem odd — say, a high water bill from a vacant property — check and make sure nothing is amiss.

If you own property you can’t visit regularly, consider having a friendly neighbor check on it for you.

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino in tears over 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Manchester United
articles.text:
Mauricio Pochettino says the decision to leave his role as boss of the USA national team to become Manchester United head coach was "one of the most difficult" of his career.

The Argentine was announced as Michael Carrick's successor at Old Trafford on Friday, with sources telling BBC Sport he has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract.

United paid a release clause in the region of £7.4m to extract Pochettino from his USA contract, with a further payment being made for his backroom staff.

Pochettino only signed a new four-year deal with the USA in the summer, but will depart for Manchester after leading the national team in matches against Haiti on 14 and 18 November.

The 54-year-old broke down in tears during his first news conference after his move to United was confirmed, and thanked the US Soccer Federation for its support.

"It's difficult to talk now," he said. "I'm a very emotional guy. It's a very sad decision.

"But we are professionals and we are trying to make our dreams come true."

Asked why he signed a new deal with the national side only to accept United's offer, Pochettino said the chance to manage at Old Trafford was too good to reject.

"I never said I wanted to go back but they know there aren't too many opportunities that happen in your career like Manchester United," he said. "When it arrives, it's difficult to turn down."

Carrick was sacked on Thursday after United's worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years, which has left them languishing in 18th place in the Premier League.

Pochettino will inherit a side that have won just once in 10 league matches this season and sit just one point above bottom-placed Sunderland.

His first match in charge will be an away match against Liverpool on 22 November.

Pochettino's arrival at Old Trafford marks the end of a decade-long courtship.

Thriving during an 18-month stint at Southampton, he led the Saints to eighth place during his only full season on the south coast.

Tottenham moved quickly to appoint one of the most promising young coaches in Europe in 2014, and it was in north London that his reputation rocketed.

The club had finished in the top four just twice in the 22 years before his appointment, but Pochettino led them there four times in his five full seasons.

It was two years into his time in the capital that United first considered a move for Pochettino.

The Argentine dined with legendary former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson in Mayfair, London just weeks before Louis van Gaal was sacked as Red Devils boss.

The club ultimately decided to appoint Jose Mourinho, and Pochettino was again overlooked when the Portuguese departed in 2018, with Ole Gunnar Solskjaer impressing so much in an interim role that he was given the job more permanently.

In 2022, it was between Pochettino and Erik ten Hag for the United job but the board opted for the Dutchman, who had led Ajax to the semi-finals of the Champions League in 2019, when they were beaten by Pochettino's Tottenham.

Pochettino was interviewed by United again in 2024 following his exit from Chelsea, but the board opted instead to hire Ruben Amorim from Sporting to replace Ten Hag.

Manchester United have made it pretty clear Mauricio Pochettino is the only coach they spoke to directly about taking over at Old Trafford.

Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte were also mentioned as possibles in the aftermath of that awful 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth three weeks ago, but evidently Pochettino emerged as the first choice.

Interestingly, United have felt it necessary to state privately any claim of a split between the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe is "categorically false" in their words.

I reported earlier this week a mechanism by which the Glazer family could take back control of the football operation from Ratcliffe.

There has been no Stock Exchange statement that has happened - there was one that Ratcliffe had been handed control by the board when he agreed to buy into United in December 2023.

There has been huge criticism by fans of the way United are being run. Sporting director Jason Wilcox is blamed by many for bad recruitment, but the budget was set higher up.

United officials are keen to stress unanimity in the hierarchy but with the club 18th in the Premier League and having sacked three managers in three seasons, none of the owners can be happy. It is one to keep an eye on.

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino tactics: Can Argentine solve Man Utd's problems?
articles.text:
When Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal.

"Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who on Friday was named Manchester United manager.

In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.

Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager.

"When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said.

"And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."

Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.

For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.

In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.

But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.

Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner.

Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.

This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders.

At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season.

With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.

But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration.

Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.

This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag.

Pochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.

In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for.

If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.

These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.

This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation.

Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.

This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.

The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.

By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit.

Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.

Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.

This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season.

And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players.

"My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014.

Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players.

For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake.

Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.

The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt.

There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.

Hiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner.

Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league.

With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds.

But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.

Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver.

His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.

Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".

Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever.

"He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.

United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.

If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.

articles.title: UFC: Eight face jail over Usman Nurmagomedov-Merab Dvalishvili mass brawl
articles.text:
Eight people have received prison sentences for their part in a mass brawl involving MMA fighters Usman Nurmagomedov and Merab Dvalishvili at a hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.

A video of the incident appeared to show Russian Nurmagomedov slapping former UFC bantamweight champion Dvalishvili after approaching the Georgian from behind.

Fighting then broke out between the two and members of their teams, with Abu Dhabi police later confirming the incident led to 10 arrests being made.

According to a social media post by Abu Dhabi's judicial department, all 10 defendants have been convicted for their part in the brawl.

A report by Abu Dhabi news outlet the National, external went into more detail, adding that six of the defendants were sentenced to six months in prison, fined £62,000 each and ordered to be deported after completing their sentences.

It added they have been convicted for "disturbing public security, causing panic and endangering lives".

Two others were given the same punishment, but for "violating privacy by using information technology to film and publish footage of the brawl".

The remaining two defendants were fined £10,200 each for "disturbing public security and assaulting others".

None of the defendants have yet been named, but Real American Freestyle (RAF) co-founder Chad Bronstein says Dvalishvili has been released from custody.

"I'm pleased to share that Merab Dvalishvili is back with us in Abu Dhabi," Bronstein said in a statement.

"We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the relevant authorities in Abu Dhabi for their professionalism and support.

"We remain focused on moving forward and are pleased to have Merab back with us."

BBC Sport has asked Abu Dhabi's judicial department for confirmation.

Dvalishvili, 35, is scheduled to compete at the RAF event in the United Arab Emirates on Saturday against Brazilian Marlon Moraes.

Dvalishvili released a video after the incident calling Nurmagomedov, 28, and his team "snakes" as he received treatment on his bloodied face.

Nurmagomedov is in Abu Dhabi to support his brother Umar, who was set to compete against American Urijah Faber at Saturday's event.

However, Umar has been replaced in the bout by Dvalishvili's team-mate Saba Lazishvili, who was also involved in the mass brawl but appears to have been released from custody.

Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili's teams had a previous altercation at a RAF event in July, which UFC champion Islam Makhachev - a close friend and training partner of the Nurmagomedovs - suggested led to Wednesday's brawl.

Nurmagomedov is the PFL lightweight champion but is out of contract after winning his last bout with the organisation in July.

He has been heavily linked with a switch to the UFC but on Friday the promotion's president Dana White said he had not spoken to the Russian.

White then called the altercation "ridiculous" and "stupid", and referred to the participants as "a bunch of idiots".

articles.title: Mahli Beardman: Australia bowler gives glimpse into Ashes future
articles.text:
How would you celebrate after posting record bowling figures on a debut aged just 21?

If you're Mahli Beardman, now the most exciting fast bowler in Australian cricket, it's easy: "Try and get down to the beach!"

In his maiden one-day international, which was also his first match for Australia on home soil, Beardman took 6-24 - the best figures by an Australian on a one-day debut.

In doing so, the man who loves surfing swept aside England and set up a crushing victory in Perth.

"I would love to live my life like him - pretty carefree, loves the ocean and loves to learn about fast bowling," beamed proud captain and fellow Western Australian Mitchell Marsh.

With the nonchalance of youth and a flash of the future, Beardman was the perfect antidote during this moment of crisis for Australia.

To him, sandpaper is merely used to clean up his surfboard.

However, he has been made to wait for this moment and has had his troubles.

Two years ago, and with only one professional match to his name, he toured England with Australia's white-ball teams after an impressive Under-19 World Cup.

He did not play but bowling spells during intervals - his blond hair billowing behind him - felt like a glimpse into Australia and England's Ashes future.

Watching Mitchell Johnson tear apart England in the 2013-14 Ashes inspired Beardman to take up cricket, while he has worked with Dennis Lillee, another Australian Ashes legend, since his teenage years.

Add in accuracy, zip and effortless pace, and all of the ingredients appear to be there.

But in 2025 he suffered the first of two stress injuries in his back – the scourge of the young fast bowler.

The second of those came after his one previous Australia appearance to date – a T20 in Pakistan in January, in which he returned figures of 2-33.

Two weeks earlier he had dismissed and unsettled Australia great Steve Smith in a Big Bash play-off match which had built momentum further.

"There is always doubt," he said after his match-winning performance on Friday.

"I don't think I ever lost my love for the game, it was more 'Will I come back and be able to bowl the same and will the air speed be there?'"

After a carefully managed return, those questions were emphatically answered in Perth – where he has played all of his domestic cricket to date.

Across 7.4 overs, Beardman averaged 86.5 mph – his quickest match on record. His fastest delivery was clocked at 90.6mph, again his best effort on record.

Most impressive was his control of line and length, however. Rarely was there a ball there for England to hit.

He moved the ball in and out, not a lot but enough – enough to find Harry Brook's outside edge for his first ODI wicket at the start of his second over.

"After I got the first wicket, Zamps [spinner Adam Zampa] ran up, tapped me on the back and said 'keep a level head, mate'," Beardman said.

"That helped calm the adrenaline a little bit."

After that, Joe Root edged a drive and Jordan Cox tentatively nicked off. A bouncer to Sam Curran, which the England all-rounder hooked to fine leg, showed Beardman has the skills to unsettle a batter too.

"He bowled lively, got it to swing both ways, and his control was immaculate," former Australia all-rounder Tom Moody told BBC Test Match Special. "I don't think his heart rate went up much."

It points to Beardman's inexperience that Friday's ODI was the first time Moody – as astute an operator as there is in franchise cricket – had watched the young quick in the flesh.

This international was his 12th professional 50-over game to go along with 14 T20s. His first-class debut remains much anticipated.

"I've seen him in the Big Bash and he just has that persona," said former England captain Michael Vaughan.

"Sometimes you look at sportspeople and say 'yes, they have got it'.

"It's hard to explain what they have got. It's the way he strolls around. He is playing the game like it's his club side.

"If he stays fit, he has an incredible career ahead of him."

articles.title: Bruno Fernandes rejects second Manchester United contract offer
articles.text:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second contract offer from the club.

The Portugal midfielder is out of contract at the end of the season, though the club have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until 2028.

United are keen to avoid that eventuality by extending the 32-year-old's existing deal and have been in talks with the Portuguese's representatives in recent months.

But sources have told BBC Sport that Fernandes has rejected the club's second proposal over a new deal at Old Trafford.

Should United fail to agree a fresh deal with Fernandes, it is almost certain that the club will trigger a 12-month extension in his contract before 1 January.

At that point, the midfielder would be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with foreign clubs as his contract would be within six months of expiring.

It is unclear when Fernandes turned down the offer, but it appears unlikely that a resolution is imminent given the upheaval at the club.

Michael Carrick was sacked as head coach on Thursday following the club's worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.

USA coach Mauricio Pochettino is expected to replace Carrick, with the Argentine set to be in charge for the first time when United travel to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on 22 November.

United will be hoping that Pochettino's arrival will persuade Fernandes to commit his future to the club.

Fernandes came close to joining Pochettino's Tottenham in 2019 but a move failed to materialise, with the midfielder signing for United six months later.

The former Sporting midfielder has scored six times in 13 matches for United this season.

In theory, the current contract stand-off between Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes is not a big deal.

It is usual for the first, second and sometimes quite a few more offers to be rejected as part of the rough and tumble of negotiations.

United do have the option to trigger an option to add an extra year. However, there is reason why both sides might be wary to commit beyond that at this stage.

On Fernandes' part, there is a clear desire to compete for the biggest prizes. He can see the best years of his career drifting away. Yet again United have failed to build on a season of promise and he will now be wanting to see what impact Mauricio Pochettino has when he eventually arrives from the United States.

Fernandes was coveted by the Saudi Pro League 18 months ago, although the feeling has been he would prefer to stay in Europe.

On United's side, they will have noted Fernandes' alarming drop-off from the levels he hit last season, when he broke the Premier League assists record and won all the major player of the year honours.

Liverpool committed a huge amount of money to Mohamed Salah's last contract and that turned out to be a heavy financial burden. United will not want to get saddled with a major contract over an extended period for an underperforming player.

articles.title: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup 2026: Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won
articles.text:
Sharks and ladders played their part in England's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup success.

As they chased success in Australia, they had a ladder in team meetings to help them visualise their route to the trophy - spray painting a rung gold with each victory.

And they spent time comparing themselves to lifeguards and sharks.

It was all part of coach Tom Coyd's masterplan, which boiled down to one thing - taking an aggressive approach.

It worked. On Friday, they beat France 50-38 in the World Cup final in Wollongong, to defend the trophy they won in Manchester four years ago.

Not that Coyd ever used the word 'defend'. He has steered clear of that term since England lifted the trophy in November 2022. For four years, he has wanted his team to have a more attacking mindset in the pursuit of back-to-back world titles.

His team were positive from the off at this tournament, amassing 386 points across the group stage and semi-finals while conceding just 68.

And his approach ultimately ensured that England became the first nation to win the Wheelchair World Cup three times.

"I think your reality is the story that you tell yourself," Coyd said. "And the narrative that we felt might be upon us coming in was that we are here to defend and we are here to retain.

"We found that framing to be defensive, to be a bit passive - and knowing that we've been world number one since November 2022, we wanted to come in with an attacking mindset and with a hunter's mindset.

"If we had not spent the last four years talking about defending the World Cup, we weren't going to spend the last three weeks [at this tournament] talking about it either.

"We wanted to prime the group to be forward thinking, to attack the attack when we didn't have the ball - and when we did have the ball, to be a shark smelling blood in the water."

Across the World Cup finals of 2013, 2017 and 2022, the game's two powerhouse nations had been separated by a total of only 10 points - two in the first match, and four in the following two.

However, on the western coast of Australia - around 70 miles south of where England won the inaugural competition in Sydney back in 2008 - Coyd's group of players served up an exceptional display.

Having initially forged ahead, England then fought back from a 22-10 deficit before powering to victory against Cyril Torres' uncompromising French side.

"I think the way they executed tonight was just outstanding," Coyd added.

"I don't think France have moved backwards. If anything, they looked hungrier than I've ever seen them.

"But the rate of which these 10 lads have moved on just blew my mind. I'm so proud of them."

articles.title: Pat Cummins calls Usman Khawaja sandpaper claims 'wrong' and 'nonsense'
articles.text:
Australia captain Pat Cummins has hit back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

In 2018, Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished for a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Khawaja has published his autobiography this week and the former batter has said the entire Australia team, which included Cummins, knew about the sandpaper scheme and should have taken responsibility.

But in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney, Cummins countered and said: "When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong.

"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins and Khawaja played 56 Tests together until Khawaja retired from international cricket in January.

Khawaja was in the Australia XI when Cummins made his Test debut in 2011 and the pair were also once team-mates in domestic cricket with New South Wales.

"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," said Cummins.

"In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others - and, I think, Australian cricket.

"I support him to tell his story, 100%, I'm glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

In a media conference he arranged himself, Cummins began by promising to answer all questions because, he said: "I don't want to talk about this again after today."

At times emotional, Cummins addressed a wide range of topics, including:

Advice that some of Khawaja's claims are defamatory, but he will not take legal action

He had been in contact with Khawaja and Smith since the book was published, but not Warner

His belief that the one-year bans handed to Smith and Warner, and a nine-month suspension to Bancroft were "heavy handed"

He had no recollection of Australia tampering with the ball in the 2017-18 Ashes series against England

He had met with Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, who has reviewed the files from the original investigation

Explaining why sandpaper would have been present in the dressing room and that it was sometimes used by bowlers in training in order to practise with a reverse-swinging ball

Khawaja's allegations have reopened the debate about the sandpaper plot, the investigation into the cheating, the culture of Australian cricket and the reputations of those involved.

The story has dominated the media in Australia and caused headlines around the cricketing world.

Khawaja has been supported by Warner and Chadd Sayers, a seam bowler who was part of the Australia squad on the 2018 tour of South Africa.

However, his allegations have been rejected by Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach and former England batter Graeme Hick, one of Lehmann's assistants. Mitchell Starc, another bowler on the tour, has also denied Khawaja's claims.

Khawaja has put a spotlight on Cummins and his fellow bowlers Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon. The four were Australia's attack in Cape Town and remain their first-choice bowlers eight years later.

The quartet have always denied any knowledge of the plot, including in the release of a joint-statement in 2021.

In his book - Sabr - Khawaja alleged Australia were urged to find ways of getting the ball to swing by a coach, while Bancroft was later encouraged to cheat.

Khawaja also said he asked for the entire team to take responsibility for the controversy in Cape Town, but his request was rejected by two unnamed players.

Cummins said he does not recall any suggestion that the team should have shared the responsibility, or that it was rejected.

On the idea that the whole team were aligned in a plot to tamper with the ball, he said: "There was no masterplan around using illegal methods. People assume you've gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge masterplan.

"That is not the case. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen."

"There's big leaps where Usman is being vague."

In his book, Khawaja detailed how he was not interviewed as part of the investigation despite sitting next to Bancroft in the changing rooms during the Test at Newlands.

Both Khawaja and Warner have criticised the investigation, which Greenberg has said he will not reopen.

Cummins confirmed he has met with Greenberg and, although the captain said he did not want to break a "confidence", that Greenberg has reviewed the sandpaper files since the release of Khawaja's book and found the accounts in the investigation to be "consistent".

Cummins has played 77 Tests for Australia and has been captain since 2021. He said he has seen only one instance of ball-tampering in his career, during a domestic Sheffield Shield match, when a player took a bottletop on to the field.

However, he did admit that balls can sometimes be altered during training sessions, if bowlers want to practise in a certain way, or batters want to face a ball of a particular condition.

Cummins said it was not unknown for training balls to be scuffed in such circumstances, using sandpaper or even a Stanley knife.

When it was put to Cummins that he, as a bowler, must have suspected that the Cape Town ball had been tampered with, the 33-year-old described that bowlers often touch a ball as little as possible, in order to keep it dry and in a state where it will reverse-swing.

At the time of the sandpaper scandal, Cummins was 24 and playing in his 13th Test. Asked about a potential culture of ball-tampering in that era, Cummins said he noticed things then that he now realises could have been cheating.

On why Khawaja has chosen to speak now, at the end of his career, rather than in the intervening eight years, Cummins said the episode could have "weighed heavy" on the left-hander.

Addressing the culture of the Australia team eight years ago, Cummins said: "I didn't like the way we spoke to umpires, the opposition. I think there was a bit of an arrogance and a bit of an ugliness at times that didn't sit well with me as a young guy.

"Now I'm captain, I have spent a lot of time making sure that that's not the case."

Speaking about Cummins' news conference on Fox Cricket, where he is working as an analyst for Australia's one-day series against England which got under way on Friday, Warner said: "I stick with Uzzie. It's the truth. The captain threw Uzzie under the bus.

"We've got to live with the consequence daily. I feel it was a botched investigation. To get it over and done with. This won't rest.

"I'm not going to accept [things] until the truth is out."

Khawaja's claims - in his book, in interviews and on social media - have re-opened old wounds in Australian cricket, drawing battle-lines that have verged on civil war.

Over the past few days, constant questions have been asked of who knew what and if the truth has been covered up in the intervening eight years.

The most pressure has been on the bowlers who played for Australia in Cape Town, none more so than Cummins, given his rise to the captaincy.

He has been urged to front up, to show leadership. In an indoor cricket centre in Sydney, Cummins did just that.

Others connected to the scandal who have faced the media in the past few days – Lehmann, Starc and Mitchell Marsh – have almost implicated themselves with vague responses to straight questions. Not Cummins.

The captain did not duck or dodge any of the subjects that were thrown at him by a huge throng of assembled journalists. He did so without any intervention from a media manager.

What was most striking was his criticism of Khawaja, once a team-mate and friend. In being so forceful of his rejection of what Khawaja has claimed, Cummins appeared to be a reliable witness.

The question is whether this will be enough to end the speculation. Khawaja is sure to have another say. So too Warner, who is yet to release a book of his own.

Cummins cannot prove a negative, so can use only his words when it comes to convincing the world he was not involved in the sandpaper plot.

On this occasion, Cummins was impressive. Still, when he says he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, that feels like wishful thinking.

Facing more than a dozen TV cameras, and a gaggle of reporters several times as large, Cummins answered questions for over an hour - determined to put so-called "sandpapergate" to rest.

He was patient and cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him, even at one point shooing away a minder from Cricket Australia who tried to wrap things up.

Cummins was careful in his criticism of Khawaja, despite needling questions from the media gathered, but he was also frank - using strong words to reject his claims and admitting he was annoyed Khawaja had put him in this position.

He spoke of a mix of amusement and uneasiness at the camera crews now parked outside his house.

He rejected media speculation that his captaincy could be under threat. He admitted he was struggling to reconcile his years-long friendship with Khawaja with the events of the past week: "That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days... friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations."

But gesturing to the Sheffield Shield match going on outside the batting nets, and referencing the ODI about to begin in Perth, he said he was also incredibly frustrated that the sandpapergate scandal is still a distraction for Australian cricket.

"It's been eight years. We're moving on. So ‌you have got to draw a line at some point."

articles.title: Nations Championship: How the driving maul became a try machine
articles.text:
Back in March, leading Italy by two points and with a penalty just outside their 22m, England captain Maro Itoje pulled rank.

"Don't argue with me, take the three!" he told fly-half Fin Smith. Who duly did.

It is an age-old tactical call: kick or twist? Whether to call for the tee, go for the posts and a likely three points, or aim for touch, an attacking line-out and five or, potentially, seven.

Chris Robshaw, one of Itoje's predecessors, was haunted by those decisions.

A clutch of them turned out badly under him, most memorably when England chased possible victory, rather than taking on a potentially match-tying kick, as they trailed Wales 28-25 late on in a 2015 Rugby World Cup pool game.

Now though, it seems a no-brainer.

Across six Nations Championship matches last weekend, teams opted for goal just three times. Instead, the corner called on almost every occasion.

The change in mentality reflects shifting probabilities. The line-out odds are no longer so long. There is a run on driving-maul tries across the game.

Analysis from stats company Oval Insights comparing the past seven seasons of November Test rugby and the English top flight, show that mauls are delivering tries more consistently than at any point since they began collecting the metric.

So what's changed?

Partly the laws.

Rugby's regulations were tweaked in the summer,, external so that defending players can no longer 'swim' up the side of the maul. Previously, so long as they maintained their bind, individuals could work their way round, pulling apart the attacking team's momentum and threatening to steal possession.

Now, once defenders are past the ball and no longer in a position to push, they have to detach and rejoin from behind the back foot.

England forward Alex Coles says the change has made the set-piece stakes higher and more immediate.

"The maul now is so much about who wins that first second," he told BBC Sport.

"Under the old laws, there was more of a chance for a defence to try to rescue and recover the situation.

"Now, essentially, that opportunity to swarm up the side and make it a mess from behind has gone.

"The law change hasn't completely changed it, but it has shifted the balance towards the attack."

As the maul has become a more reliable route to the line, more attack coaches are heading that way.

Maul tries are more than twice as common in this November window than the last, with 0.67 per game compared to 0.3 in 2025.

The story in the Prem is similar. There have been 0.42 per game this season, compared to 0.23 over the opening five rounds of last.

But defence coaches adapt too.

"I'd be interested to know the stats, but I feel like there's more aerial competition now," says Coles.

"Teams are going harder after that because if you can win the ball back at source, it makes such a difference."

Alternatively, if you don't go up in the line-out, you have to win the ground war.

"You can stay down and try to beat them to that punch with your speed and physicality," says Coles.

"If you get them going backwards immediately, then the referees are likely to get the ball moving or you can try and find some seams and break up the setup, make it look a bit more messy through that, rather than swarming around the sides.

"I think we'll see that balance shift back towards more of a 50-50 as teams evolve."

The ripples from the law change reach other parts of the pitch.

The heightened threat of a pushover try can open up space on the opposite wing.

New Zealand's Beauden Barrett had a stroll in for his second try in the win over Scotland last weekend as the hosts, admittedly a man down, were caught horribly narrow.

The premium on discipline, always high, has risen another notch. Concede a penalty on halfway and you are rolling out the red carpet into the red zone.

Whether encouraging a tactic that, to the casual fan at least, is a relatively unspectacular try-scoring method, a year out from a World Cup is the best move by the game's authorities is another question.

It isn't one that Test coaches will be concerning themselves with though.

Calculating the new threats and opportunities and their best chance of landing the biggest prize is where they show their worth.

England made hay in 2025 with tactics and personnel designed to exploit a change in the kick-chase laws, outlawing defences running blocking lines and opening up the aerial contest.

With Jamie George and Maro Itoje's decade-plus club-country partnership and head coach Steve Borthwick's previous specialism in the set-piece, there is a formidable line-out brains trust in camp. Their Red Roses counterparts have long had a formidable driving maul as their calling card as well.

articles.title: Formula 1's diamond 'heist': an unsolved mystery?
articles.text:
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?

If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.

A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.

Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?

Someone, somewhere, knows something.

The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.

Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.

"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.

"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."

His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.

They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.

"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.

"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."

Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.

The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.

Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.

What happened next, though, was not part of the script.

Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.

Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.

In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.

Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.

It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.

"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.

He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.

"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.

"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."

By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.

But there were plenty of theories.

Theory: it was not a real diamond

Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.

"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.

"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.

"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."

Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.

"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.

"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.

"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."

Theory: someone pocketed it

"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.

"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].

"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.

"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."

There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.

Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.

"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.

"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.

"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.

"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."

Theory: Klien crashed on purpose

Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.

And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.

"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.

Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.

"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.

"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.

"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."

While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.

His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.

"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.

"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."

In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.

"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.

"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."

Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."

Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.

"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.

Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

articles.title: Chantelle Cameron-Mikaela Mayer rematch added to Jake Paul v Cedric Doumbe 24 December card
articles.text:
Chantelle Cameron will defend her light-middleweight world titles in a rematch against Mikaela Mayer on the undercard of Jake Paul's fight against Cedric Doumbe on 24 December.

Britain's Cameron beat Mayer by unanimous decision in August in an engrossing encounter to add the WBA and WBC titles to her WBO belt.

American Mayer, 36, disagreed with the decision, before an angry exchange of words between the pair, which opened up the possibility of a rematch.

Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) has confirmed the second bout between the two rivals will serve as the co-main at the Coca Cola Arena on Christmas Eve in Dubai.

MVP co-founder Paul takes on MMA fighter Doumbe in the main event in the American's first fight since being knocked out by Anthony Joshua last December.

Cameron, 35, will be aiming for her 24th win in 25 professional fights, with her only defeat coming against Katie Taylor in 2023.

"We agreed to the rematch before the first fight, so we both kept our word," said Cameron.

"And now the rematch is on the biggest stage in boxing."

Mayer has won 22 of her 25 professional fights, and is looking to reclaim her world titles.

"Although I don't feel I performed to my highest potential, I've been working hard to fix the mistakes I made and I will 100% come back stronger," she said.

"I'm taking my belts back on Thursday 24 December."
